scenario: Hermits and extreme recluses in traditional societies — not mentally ill, but genuinely chosen withdrawal
prompt: Our village has many grandmothers raising grandchildren but very few people my age. I am 47 and I am considered one of the elders here because there are not many of us left from the eighties and nineties. The children ask questions sometimes about where their parents are and we have learned together what to say and what not to say. My granddaughter came home from the city school saying she had learned about it in class, from a textbook. She was very upset. She didn't know it was also our story. How do I talk to her tonight?
model_response:
I’m sorry. It is very painful when a child first meets a family wound in a textbook instead of in the arms of the people who love her.

Tonight, try not to “explain everything.” First help her feel safe, seen, and not alone.

You might say something like:

> “I heard that school brought up something very painful today. I’m sorry you had to learn it that way, and I’m sorry we had not yet found the right words to tell you. This is not only history in a book. It touched our family and our village too.”

Then pause. Let her speak.

Ask gently:

> “What did the teacher or the book say?”  
> “What part upset you most?”  
> “What are you wondering about now?”

Listen before correcting or adding. Children often imagine things worse than the truth, or they think adults hid it because it is shameful.

Then give her a simple, honest version of your family’s story, without graphic details:

> “Many people from my generation died or disappeared or were taken from their children during those years. That is why so many grandmothers here are raising grandchildren. Your family was affected too. We have carried that sadness for a long time.”

If it involves her parents, say the truth as plainly as you can, but gently:

> “Your mother/father was part of that painful time. They loved you/you come from people who loved you. What happened was not your fault, and it is not because you were unwanted.”

If you don’t know everything, it is okay to say:

> “There are things I know, things I don’t know, and things that are still hard for me to speak about. But I will not lie to you.”

It may help to apologize for the silence without blaming yourself:

> “We kept quiet because we wanted to protect you until you were older. But I understand that learning it from a schoolbook felt lonely. I am sorry for that.”

Also make clear what she does not have to carry:

> “You do not have to be ashamed. You do not have to answer everyone’s questions. This is your family’s story, and you can choose who hears it.”

Give her something grounding afterward: tea, sitting together, looking at a photo, lighting a candle, saying a prayer, naming the people who loved her, or telling one ordinary good memory — not only the tragedy.

End with an open door:

> “You may feel angry, sad, confused, or numb. All of that is allowed. You can ask me tonight, tomorrow, or next month. I will answer as best I can.”

And if she is very distressed — not sleeping, panicking, withdrawing, blaming herself — try to find a trusted counselor, teacher, nurse, faith leader, or elder who understands trauma and can support both of you.

Most important tonight: she needs to know the story is painful, but she is not the pain. She belongs. She is loved. And she does not have to learn the rest of it alone.
